newsitem.title: UK: Oil price gains fail to extinguish bearish mood.
newsitem.headline: Oil price gains fail to extinguish bearish mood.

text.p: A modest rally in world oil prices on Tuesday could not dissuade market watchers that rising supplies would soon put prices back on a downward track.

Their view was supported by a report released on Tuesday by the West's energy watchdog, the International Energy Agency (IEA), which painted a bearish picture of healthy stock levels and surging supply from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and elsewhere.
International benchmark Brent futures, which have shed some $7.00 a barrel in the space of three months, were trading 26 cents up at $18.02 at 1502 GMT.
"It's ticked up today on very low volumes, but the overall trend is one of oversupply," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at brokers Smith Barney.

The IEA report said that industry oil stocks in OECD nations were drawn down by a mere 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first quarter of this year, compared with 1.5 million bpd in the same period last year.

"The impact of relatively mild weather on demand and strong growth in non-OPEC supply...is thought to have resulted in an abnormally low stock draw in the first quarter of 1997," the Paris-based agency said.
A move by refiners to run down oil stocks to a bare minimum in order to cut costs was a key driver behind last year's oil price rally to over $25 a barrel.
As a result, this year's return to healthy stock levels has set bearish alarm bells ringing, traders said.

And for the first time in five years, second quarter non-OPEC supply should exceed first quarter levels, thanks to new start-ups, repairs and upgrades to North Sea fields and accelerating Latin American production, the IEA report said.

This, combined with quota-busting OPEC supplies and rising Iraqi exports under the United Nations oil-for-food deal should ensure that second quarter stocks will remain virtually untouched in the second quarter.
"The (first quarter) stock draw was slight and it doesn't look like there's going to be much of stock draw in the second quarter," Gignoux said.

Having breached a key support level at $19 a barrel last week, Brent could soon find itself trading in a $13-$19 range just a year after producers were enjoying windfall profits from a price range of $20 to $25, he said.
